about.title: East Palo Alto Slip & Fall Claims
about.longDescription: East Palo Alto is a compact, busy city where people move between corridors like University Avenue, E Bayshore Road, and Bay Road for shopping, transit, and daily errands. Falls happen in the places locals rely on every day: grocery store aisles, apartment stairwells near Bay Road, parking lots off US-101, and sidewalks along University Avenue. Under California law, a property owner or manager isn't automatically responsible just because someone fell on their property. The injured person generally has to show the owner knew, or reasonably should have known, about the hazard and didn't fix it or warn about it. That's why what happens right after a fall matters. Photos of the spill, broken step, or torn carpet, along with any surveillance footage, can shape whether a claim holds up. LawProactive doesn't practice law. We simply connect you, free of charge, with an independent attorney who can evaluate what happened and explain your options.

whyChoose.title: Why This Matters Under California Law

items.title: Notice Is the Core Issue
items.desc: California requires showing the property owner knew or should have known about the hazard and failed to address it. An attorney can help gather evidence, like maintenance logs or prior complaints, that speaks to this.

items.title: Surveillance Video Disappears Fast
items.desc: Many East Palo Alto retailers and apartment complexes overwrite security footage within days or weeks. Acting quickly to request preservation of that video can be critical to a claim.

items.title: Comparative Fault Can Reduce, Not Erase, Recovery
items.desc: California uses pure comparative fault, meaning even if you're found partly responsible for the fall, you may still recover a reduced amount rather than nothing at all.

items.question: How long do I have to file a premises liability claim in East Palo Alto?
items.answer: Generally, California gives you two years from the date of the fall to file a lawsuit. If the property involved is owned by a public entity, such as a city building or school, the deadline is much shorter and requires an early formal claim. An independent attorney can help sort out which timeline applies to your situation.

items.question: What if the store or landlord says I wasn't paying attention?
items.answer: That's a common response, but California's comparative fault rule means partial responsibility doesn't automatically bar you from recovering compensation. It may reduce the amount, but an attorney can help evaluate the actual facts, like lighting, warning signs, or how long the hazard existed.

items.question: I fell near University Avenue but didn't report it right away. Is it too late?
I fell near University Avenue but didn't report it right away. Is it too late?
items.answer: It's not automatically too late, but delays can make it harder to gather surveillance footage or witness accounts before they're lost. The sooner you connect with an attorney, the better the chance of preserving evidence like store camera footage or maintenance records tied to the specific location.
